name: Thoracodorsal nerve
summary: The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C6, C7, C8) between the subscapular nerves, descends along the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal artery and enters the latissimus dorsi, which it supplies. It is at risk in axillary lymph node dissection and in posterior shoulder surgery, it is the nerve of the latissimus flap used in reconstruction, and its EMG places lesions in the posterior cord: latissimus weakness with radial and axillary signs means the posterior cord, whereas latissimus sparing points to the individual nerves.

anatomy.location: Leaves the posterior cord in the axilla between the upper and lower subscapular nerves, descends along the posterior axillary wall on the surface of the subscapularis and teres major with the thoracodorsal artery, and enters the deep surface of the latissimus dorsi near its tendon.

function: Motor to the latissimus dorsi, it adducts, extends and medially rotates the arm and pulls the body up in climbing and in transfers from a wheelchair, and it contributes to forced expiration and coughing; its loss weakens adduction against resistance (the patient cannot press the arm down against the examiner's hand) and is felt most by athletes and by paraplegics who depend on the latissimus for transfers. Its origin from the posterior cord makes it a cord marker in plexus lesions, and surgeons preserve it during axillary clearance or use it, with its artery, as the pedicle of the latissimus flap for breast and chest wall reconstruction and for restoring elbow flexion after brachial plexus injury.

bestView.label: thoracodorsal nerve along the posterior axillary wall to the latissimus dorsi
nerve with the thoracodorsal artery on the subscapularis

imaging.normalAppearance: A nerve accompanying the thoracodorsal vessels on the posterior axillary wall on ultrasound and MRI; denervation appears as STIR change and atrophy of the latissimus dorsi.

pathology.finding: Denervation of the latissimus dorsi with the deltoid, teres minor and radial-innervated muscles, placing the lesion in the posterior cord.
Latissimus dorsi denervation edema and later atrophy after axillary surgery, with weak adduction.
Absent latissimus in the back after reconstruction, with the muscle transposed to the chest wall on its thoracodorsal pedicle.

lesionEffects.deficit: Weak adduction and extension of the arm
Difficulty with climbing, pulling and wheelchair transfers
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the latissimus contribution to body elevation
Origin from the posterior cord with the axillary and radial nerves

examination: Adduction of the abducted arm against resistance while palpating the latissimus in the posterior axillary fold
Cough strength in patients with bilateral involvement
EMG of the latissimus in suspected posterior cord lesions
pearls: The latissimus is the muscle of climbing and of transfers; its nerve is the one axillary surgeons protect
Latissimus plus deltoid plus wrist drop means the posterior cord
The thoracodorsal pedicle carries the latissimus to the chest wall in reconstruction
